PENDING NON-BAILABLE WARRANT IS NOT AN ABSOLUTE BAR TO SEEKING VIRTUAL APPEARANCE – GAUHATI HIGH COURT

In an important development towards technology-enabled criminal justice, the Gauhati High Court recognised that an accused facing a Non-Bailable Warrant (NBW) can seek permission to appear virtually under Section 530 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS).

Case: Shivam Pandey v. State of Assam
Citation: 2026:GAU-AS:17113
Case No.: Crl.Pet./1575/2026
Date of Judgment: 19 November 2026

FACTS OF THE CASE

The accused, who had previously been granted bail, failed to appear before the Trial Court, resulting in the issuance of a Non-Bailable Warrant. Citing medical difficulties and geographical distance, the accused sought permission to appear through video conferencing.

KEY LEGAL ISSUE

Whether the existence of a Non-Bailable Warrant prevents an accused from seeking permission to participate in criminal proceedings through electronic mode under Section 530 BNSS.

HIGH COURT OBSERVATIONS

▪️ Section 530 BNSS provides a statutory framework for conducting criminal proceedings through electronic mode.

▪️ An outstanding NBW does not automatically preclude an accused from seeking virtual appearance.

▪️ The Court permitted the accused to submit fresh applications seeking virtual appearance and regular bail before the Trial Court.

▪️ Such applications must be considered in accordance with law and the circumstances of the case.

PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE

This judgment assumes particular relevance in criminal proceedings, including cheque dishonour cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, where accused persons may reside in different states or face genuine difficulties in attending proceedings physically.

However, virtual appearance is not an absolute right, nor does it automatically result in the cancellation of an NBW or restoration of bail.

LEGAL TAKEAWAY

Technology should facilitate access to justice without compromising procedural discipline, judicial discretion or the effective administration of criminal law.

The judgment reflects the evolving landscape of India's criminal justice system, where physical presence need not invariably be the only means of judicial participation.

Dhaval Sudhir Bhatt
Advocate | LL.M. | ACIArb (UK)
Member – Supreme Court Bar Association

AONE JUSTITIA | Advocates & Associates

Published in public interest for legal awareness and academic discussion.
comment: The practical challenge will be ensuring virtual appearance is not used to sidestep an outstanding NBW. Clear safeguards around identity verification, undertakings and future attendance could help courts balance access with accountability.
